appraisal_events.evidence: Charlus ne me trompa... que parce qu'il s'y trompait lui-même... il ne faisait rien, n'écrivait pas, ne peignait pas, ne lisait même rien d'une manière sérieuse... Mais, supérieur aux gens du monde de plusieurs degrés... il n'était pas pour cela compris par eux... il pouvait tout au plus dégager le charme fallacieux des gens du monde... pour les artistes seulement.
appraisal_events.explanation: The narrator judges Charlus as self-deceived and intellectually unproductive, yet also credits him with a perceptiveness superior to society people that goes unrecognized by them and is fully useful only to artists, via the reindeer/Eskimo simile.

appraisal_events.evidence: faisant oublier à celle-ci combien la réalité l'avait déçue chez la Mme de Guermantes... l'avaient aiguillée vers la cousine de Mme de Guermantes
appraisal_events.explanation: The narrator recalls that the lived reality of visiting the duchesse's salon had disappointed the earlier imaginative mystique attached to her, which is why his fantasy migrated to her cousin, the princesse.

status_effects.explanation: Portrayed as self-deceived and unproductive (writes nothing, paints nothing, reads nothing seriously), which lowers the narrator's esteem for him despite his social insight.

Credited by the narrator with a perceptiveness several degrees above society people and a genuine (if fallacious) charm he alone can extract and pass on to artists, even though society itself fails to understand him.
The narrator's earlier imaginative mystique about her is deflated by the disappointing reality of actually knowing her, prompting his fantasy to shift elsewhere.

ambiguities: The extended judgment of Charlus (self-deceived dilettante vs. artist-adjacent superior perceiver) reads as the narrator's own analytic voice, but given Charlus's broader characterization elsewhere in the novel it could alternatively be read with more ironic distance than scored here.
